rv.q: Part Two finds its footing and doesn’t take one wrong step: the humour working brilliantly in occasional flecks, the drama leading with emotion, thought and the everyday tragedy of marital disappointment.
They have condensed and reshaped a literary treasure to produce a theatrical marvel on an epic scale.
This vivid and emotional adaptation is definitely a theatrical highlight of the year so far, and further evidence that bringing more books to the stage is the way forward.
This is a lovely piece of theatre, rich with the empathy that characterises Eliot’s much-loved original.
Inevitably perhaps, much is missing – for me, the depths of Dorothea's despair and disappointment. But it is nevertheless an awesome achievement, well worth seeing.
What makes the whole entirely compelling is its fluidity and grace and the sheer calibre of the acting.
I suspect only the most passionate Eliot devotees would want to see this production, directed by Jeremy Herrin, in a single day.
Jeremy Herrin's fleet, sparely designed production impresses, as secrets spill and paths intersect.

cn.t: Critics praise the RSC's ambitious adaptation of George Eliot's masterpiece as a deftly clever achievement, with a beautifully energetic ensemble bringing humor and compassion to the sprawling novel across six compelling hours of theater.
